note: Persons of interest. A person is on the board because a card names them. Cards reference people by id in `people`; the site also matches `name` and `aka` in a card's text, so most appearances are found without tagging. `role` is one line; `bio` is what the file says about them, in the board's voice — no biography beyond what bears on the case.

people.name: David Hilbert
people.bio: Posed the twenty-three problems in 1900 that set the century's agenda, and the programme — to put all of mathematics on a finite, checkable footing — that Gödel and Turing answered in the negative.

people.name: Kurt Gödel
people.bio: Proved in 1931 that any consistent formal system rich enough for arithmetic contains true statements it cannot prove. The result is the fence around everything a machine can be asked to decide.

people.name: Alan Turing
people.bio: Defined computation in 1936 and asked in 1950 whether machines can think, proposing that the question be replaced by a test. Both papers are on the board; nearly everything else descends from one or the other.

people.name: Claude Shannon
people.bio: Showed in 1937 that switching circuits do Boolean algebra, and in 1948 gave information a unit. The second paper is why a model's output can be measured in bits and its training in loss.

people.name: Warren McCulloch
people.bio: With Walter Pitts, modelled the nerve cell as a logic gate in 1943 — the first neural network on paper, and the reason the word 'neuron' survived into the deep-learning decade.

people.name: Donald Hebb
people.bio: Proposed in 1949 that cells that fire together wire together. Every learning rule on the board, backpropagation included, is a formalisation of the idea.

people.name: John McCarthy
people.bio: Coined 'artificial intelligence' for the 1956 Dartmouth proposal and invented Lisp two years later. The field's name, and its first language, are his.

people.name: Marvin Minsky
people.bio: Built the first neural-network learning machine in 1951 and, with Seymour Papert, wrote the 1969 book that was read as closing the door on neural networks for a decade. Both cards are his.

people.name: Frank Rosenblatt
people.bio: Built the perceptron in 1957 and promised the Navy a machine that would walk, talk and see. The promise was the first the field could not keep; the machine was the ancestor of every network since.

people.name: Herbert Simon
people.bio: With Newell and Shaw wrote Logic Theorist, the first program to prove theorems, and predicted in 1957 that a computer would be world chess champion within ten years. He was forty years early.

people.name: Allen Newell
people.bio: Co-author of Logic Theorist and the General Problem Solver, and of the idea that intelligence is search through a space of symbols — the programme that dominated the field until statistics won.

people.name: Arthur Samuel
people.bio: Wrote a checkers program in 1952 that improved by playing itself, and in 1959 gave the technique its name: machine learning.

people.name: Joseph Weizenbaum
people.bio: Wrote ELIZA in 1966 and was alarmed when people confided in it. He spent the rest of his career warning about the confusion the board keeps recording.

people.name: James Lighthill
people.bio: Wrote the 1973 report for the British Science Research Council that found the field had not delivered on its promises. Funding stopped; the first winter is dated from it.

people.name: John Hopfield
people.bio: Brought neural networks back in 1982 with a network that stores memories as energy minima. The Nobel forty-two years later cites that paper.

people.name: Geoffrey Hinton
people.bio: On the 1986 backpropagation paper, the 2006 deep-belief-network paper, the 2012 AlexNet paper, and the 2013 auction that sold his three-person company to Google. Left Google in 2023 to speak about risk. The board's most-connected person.

people.name: Yann LeCun
people.bio: Made convolutional networks read handwriting in 1989 and was hired by Zuckerberg in 2013 to run Meta's AI research. Turing Award 2018 with Hinton and Bengio; the board's loudest sceptic of the risk case.

people.name: Yoshua Bengio
people.bio: The third of the 2018 Turing laureates, on the GAN paper, and after 2023 the most senior researcher to call for a pause and to chair the international scientific report on AI safety.

people.name: Jürgen Schmidhuber
people.bio: With Sepp Hochreiter, published the LSTM in 1997 — the recurrent network that ran language and speech until the transformer replaced it.

people.name: Fei-Fei Li
people.bio: Built ImageNet — fourteen million labelled images — when the field thought data was the boring part. The 2012 result that started the decade was on her benchmark.

people.name: Jensen Huang
people.bio: Opened graphics chips to general computation with CUDA in 2007 and sold the shovels for every training run since. In 2024 his company became the most valuable on earth.

people.name: Ilya Sutskever
people.bio: On the AlexNet paper, on sequence-to-sequence, co-founder and chief scientist of OpenAI, one of the board members who removed Altman in 2023, and gone within six months. His name is on four rungs of the board.

people.name: Demis Hassabis
people.role: Chief executive · Google DeepMind, Nobel chemistry 2024
people.bio: Founded DeepMind in 2010, sold it to Google in 2014, and led the teams behind AlphaGo, AlphaZero, AlphaFold and the olympiad results. The Nobel is for AlphaFold.

people.name: David Silver
people.bio: Led AlphaGo and AlphaZero — the self-play recipe that the reasoning models of 2025 returned to.

people.name: Sam Altman
people.bio: Co-founded OpenAI with Musk in 2015, took it capped-profit in 2019, launched ChatGPT in 2022, was fired and rehired in five days in 2023, and converted the company in 2025. The board's power thread mostly runs through him.

people.name: Elon Musk
people.bio: Co-founded OpenAI as a counterweight to Google, left its board in 2018, sued it in 2024 over the abandonment of the mission, and founded a rival. On the board he is the string that provoked the string.

people.name: Greg Brockman
people.bio: Co-founder of OpenAI who resigned in solidarity when Altman was fired in 2023 and returned with him.

people.name: Dario Amodei
people.bio: Led research at OpenAI through GPT-2 and GPT-3, left in 2021 with a group of colleagues to found Anthropic, and has since published the labs' most detailed public risk assessments alongside the models.

people.name: Timnit Gebru
people.bio: Co-led Google's ethical AI team until a dispute over a paper on the risks of large language models ended in her departure in 2020. The paper's title — stochastic parrots — outlived the dispute.

people.name: Mark Zuckerberg
people.bio: Hired LeCun in 2013 and in 2023–24 made Meta the lab that gives frontier weights away, arguing that AI would go the way of Linux. The open-weights side of the board is largely his.

people.name: Garry Kasparov
people.bio: Lost to Deep Blue in 1997 and has argued ever since that the match proved less than it seemed. The board's model for how every later victory was received.

people.name: Lee Sedol
people.bio: Lost four games to one against AlphaGo in 2016, won the fourth with a move the machine had not considered, and retired in 2019 saying AI could not be defeated.

people.name: Ray Kurzweil
people.bio: Put 2045 on the poster as the year of the singularity. The board keeps the date as a scenario card, on manila stock, with the confidence it deserves.

people.name: François Chollet
people.bio: Built the ARC benchmark in 2019 to resist memorisation and staked a million-dollar prize on it in 2024. It fell to compute and stands on efficiency — the one game the board says is still open.

people.name: Terence Tao
people.bio: The mathematician the field checks its claims with. Reviewed FrontierMath, tracked the Erdős problems as machines began to solve them, and warned against simple comparisons when the olympiad fell.

people.name: Paul Erdős
people.bio: Left more than a thousand open problems, catalogued and numbered. In 2025–26 they became the field's test of whether a machine could do research rather than pass an exam.

people.name: Noam Brown
people.bio: Built Libratus and Pluribus, the poker programs, then took the search-plus-learning recipe to OpenAI's reasoning models.

people.name: Tuomas Sandholm
people.bio: Brown's adviser and co-author on Libratus and Pluribus; the game-theory side of the poker results.

people.name: Jonathan Schaeffer
people.bio: Built Chinook, which took the checkers title in 1994, and led the eighteen-year computation that solved the game in 2007.

people.name: Victoria Krakovna
people.bio: Keeps the list of specification-gaming examples that gave the behaviour a name and the gaming-the-test lead its second rung.

people.name: Dan Hendrycks
people.bio: Wrote the MATH benchmark in 2021 and organised the 2023 one-sentence statement on extinction risk signed by the heads of the major labs.

people.name: Blake Lemoine
people.bio: Said in 2022 that Google's LaMDA was sentient, and was dismissed. The first public case of a professional convinced by a system he was testing.

people.name: Liang Wenfeng
people.bio: Funded DeepSeek from a quantitative hedge fund and released R1 in January 2025 — the open-weight reasoning model that reset the price of the frontier.
